main.text: Since it appears from what has been said so far that the raven is a base and abject animal, and hateful to men, some wonder why sacred Scripture so often and so explicitly testifies that ravens are a care to God. Thus Iob. XXXIX, 3. (var. XXXVIII, 41.): Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry to God, wandering for lack of food? And Psal. CXLVII, (var. CXLVI,) 9. Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young of the ravens that cry. And Luc. XII, 24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Nor do many of the ancients allow these passages to be understood literally. To call upon God (says Hilary on Psalm 146) is the proper office of man. But how do the young of ravens call upon God? And why the young of ravens rather than the ravens etc.? Or what food is supplied? Will God, as he gives hay to the beasts and grass to men, so bestow the stinking filth of rotting carcasses and the deaths of cattle as food for the present life on the young ravens that pray to him? To understand these things so is, I will not say an error, but the height of irreligion. And Augustine: Shall we perhaps think this, that ravens call upon God to give them food? Do not imagine this, that an irrational soul calls upon God etc. Take what is said as a figure. And the author of the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome: Answer, Jew, answer, you who follow only the Jewish letter. Do you say these ravens are truly ravens? If then it is written of the young of ravens, „And to the young of ravens calling upon him;“ and it is written Ioel. II. ^{a)}, Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved: then the young of ravens too will be saved in the resurrection. And so the sacred Doctors take refuge in allegories as in a sacred anchor. By ravens they understand the gentiles; by the young of ravens, Christians, who, though sprung from the gentiles, [col. 204] nevertheless call upon the true God. But, if I may say so with their leave, allegories do not destroy the literal sense but presuppose it. I would therefore not indulge in them before the literal sense is established. If we reject it in these passages, nothing in Scripture will be certain, nothing that cannot easily be twisted elsewhere. For why should we not admit that Job in chapter 39 treated of real ravens just as of real ibexes, lions, wild asses, horses, eagles, ostriches etc. in what follows or precedes in this same chapter? Since in so many descriptions of animals we freely admit that the rest are taken literally, why should this one alone contain nothing that is not allegorical? So too in these words of David, Who gives to the beasts their food, and to the young [II, 795] of the ravens that cry: since the first part of the verse signifies real beasts, why should the latter not also signify real ravens? And in Christ's words, Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap etc., that birds are meant, not men, is plainly shown 1. by comparing this passage with the parallel Matth. VI, 26. Behold the birds of the air, which do not sow, nor reap, etc. 2. Because they are denied to sow, reap and have barns into which to gather their produce. 3. Because at the end of the verse Christ adds, How much more are you worth than the birds? as in Luke; or, Are you not of much more value than they? as in Matthew. 4. Finally, if ravens or birds are understood allegorically, the lilies in what follows will not be real lilies either, but whatever it pleases τοῖς ἀλληγορηταῖς [tois allēgorētais] to invent. Let this therefore stand certain, that in the passages we have cited real ravens are meant. Nor should anyone be moved by the objection from the Psalm, τοῖς νεοσσοῖς τῶν κοράκων τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτὸν [tois neossois tōn korakōn tois epikaloumenois auton], to the young of ravens calling upon him, since the Hebrew has only that God gives his food לבני עורב אשר יקראו, to the sons of the raven, which cry. This is followed by the Chaldee, the Syriac, and Jerome's version. But, after the Greeks, the Vulgate translator, the Ethiopic, and the two Arabic versions added the pronoun, as if the Prophet had expressly said that the young of ravens call upon God, or cry to God. Yet if anyone thinks that after David's words, to the young of ravens that cry, one should supply to God, I will not strongly contest it, since in Job the young of ravens are explicitly said to cry to God: but in the sense in which young lions are said to roar after their prey, and to seek their food from God, Psal. CIV, 21; and the eyes of all animals to look to God, who gives them their food in its season, Psal. CXLV, 15; and the beasts of the field to cry out to him, because the watercourses are dried up, Ioel. I, 20. Rightly therefore Theodoret: Οὐ λογικὴ τῶν κοράκων ἡ φύσις, οὐδ᾽ ὅτι λογικῶς ἐπικαλεῖται τὸν ποιητήν· ἀλλ᾽ ἡ διὰ τὴν χρείαν κραυγὴ μιμεῖται τὴν αἴτησιν [Ou logikē tōn korakōn hē physis, oud᾽ hoti logikōs epikaleitai ton poiētēn; all᾽ hē dia tēn chreian kraugē mimeitai tēn aitēsin]. The nature of ravens is not rational, nor does it call upon its maker by the guidance of reason: but the cry uttered from need imitates a petition. Elias of Crete copied this almost word for word in his Notes on Gregory's Oration 51. And the metaphor, elegant everywhere, is the more elegant where ravens are concerned, because, while most birds seem to celebrate God with their song and to sing hymns εὐχαριστικοὺς [eucharistikous] in his praise, the raven has a clamorous and noisy voice, like an importunate beggar. And in fact it is believed sometimes to ask for alms with its croaking. Hence (as Aelian relates, History book 2, ch. 48) Κόρακες Αἰγύπτιοι, ὅσοι τῷ Νείλῳ προσδιαιτῶνται, τῶν πλεόντων ἐοίκασιν ἱκέται εἶναι, λαβεῖν τι αἰτοῦντες [Korakes Aigyptioi, hosoi tō Neilō prosdiaitōntai, tōn pleontōn eoikasin hiketai einai, labein ti aitountes], the Egyptian ravens that live along the Nile seem to be suppliants, as it were, of those sailing by, begging that something be given them. And in Hesychius: Κοράξαι, ἄγαν προσλιπαρῆσαι· πεποίηται παρὰ τοὺς κόρακας [Koraxai, agan prosliparēsai; pepoiētai para tous korakas] (I would prefer παρὰ τοῦ κόρακος [para tou korakos]). By these words he means that τὸ κοράξαι [to koraxai] is the same as to ask insistently, and that the word is taken from ravens. And Suidas under Κοράττειν [Korattein] adds the reason, saying it was taken ἀπὸ τῶν περὶ τὰς θύρας κοράκων περιπετομένων, [II, 796] καὶ μὴ ἀποχωρούντων [apo tōn peri tas thyras korakōn peripetomenōn, kai mē apochōrountōn], from ravens which (seeking something) fly around the doors of houses and do not depart from there.

But, they ask, why do Job and David attribute this demand for food not to the ravens themselves, but to the chicks of the ravens? [col. 205] To answer this question the Hebrews and Arabs devise many things, as will be clear from what follows. Rabbi Eliezer in the Capitula, near the end of ch. 21: When the ravens have hatched their chicks and see that they are white, they flee from them, thinking that they are the young of a serpent; then God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, grants them food without want. R. Selomo on Job: יתעו מבלי אכל שאביהם שונאם והקב״ה מזמן להם יתושים הנבראים מצואתן ונכנסין לתוך פיהם, They wander without food, because they are hateful to their father; but God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, prepares for them gnats, generated from their own dung, which enter into their mouth. Aben Ezra on Psalm CXLVII.: חכמי הגויים אומרים כי אבותם יעזבום בהולדם, The philosophers of the gentiles assert that they are deserted by their parents as soon as they are born. And Kimchi: לפי שהם לבנים בהולדם ואמותיהם מניחים אותם ולא יביאו להם טרפם כי יחשבו כי אינם בניהם לפי שהם לבנים והם צווחים כאלו יקראו לאל בעד טרפם והקב״ה מזמין להם יתושין ואוכלים אותם, because they are born white, their mothers desert them and do not bring them food; for they do not recognize them as their own, since they are white. Therefore they cry out, as if they were asking God for their food. And God prepares gnats for them to feed on. So much for the Hebrews; now hear the Arabs. Among them the poet Hariri sings thus in مقامة [maqāma] Mekama, or stantia, 13.
يا رازق النعاب في عشه [yā rāziq al-naʿʿāb fī ʿushshihi] وجابر العظم الكسير المهيض [wa-jābir al-ʿaẓm al-kasīr al-mahīḍ]

O you who nourish the raven in its nest, and repair the broken and crushed jaw of the wild ass. The first part of this distich the Scholiast attributes to David, and explains it thus: الغراب اذا فقس عن فراخه خرجت بيضا فاذا راها ابواها كذلك نفرا عنها فتفتح افواها فيرسل الله تبارك وتعالي لها ذبابا فيدخل في افواها فيركون لها غذا حتي تسود فاذا اسودت عاد ابواها اليها فغذياها ويرفع الله الذباب عنها [al-ghurāb idhā faqasa ʿan firākhihi kharajat bīḍan fa-idhā raʾāhā abawāhā ka-dhālika nafarā ʿanhā fa-taftaḥ afwāhā fa-yursil Allāh tabāraka wa-taʿālī lahā dhubāban fa-yadkhul fī afwāhā fa-yarkūn lahā ghidhā ḥattī taswadd fa-idhā iswaddat ʿāda abawāhā ilayhā fa-ghadhdhayāhā wa-yarfaʿ Allāh al-dhubāb ʿanhā] When the raven hatches its chicks, they come out white. When the parents see them so, they take to flight. But the chicks open their mouths, and God, blessed and exalted, sends them flies, which, entering their mouths, serve them as food until they turn black. Only then do the parents return and feed them, and God removes the flies from them. Alkazuinius teaches the same in words little different. And Damir somewhat more fully: اذا خرجت الفراخ [II, 797] الغراخ من البيض طردتها لانها تخرج قبيحة المنظر حدا انا تكون صغار الاجرام عظيم الروس والمناقر جرد اللون الاجساد متفواتا الاعضا فالابوان [idhā kharajat al-firākh al-ghirākh min al-bayḍ ṭaradathā li-annahā takhruj qabīḥat al-manẓar ḥadā anā takūn ṣighār al-ajrām ʿaẓīm al-rūs wa-al-manāqir jurd al-lawn al-ajsād mutafawwatā al-aʿḍā fa-al-abawān] [col. 206] ينظران الفرخ كذلك فيتركانه فيجعل الله تعالي قوته في الذباب والبعوض الكاين في عشه الي ان يقوي وينبت ريشه فيعود اليه ابواه فيرزقانه [yanẓurān al-farkh ka-dhālika fa-yatrukānih fa-yajʿal Allāh taʿālī qūtah fī al-dhubāb wa-al-baʿūḍ al-kāyin fī ʿushshih ilī an yaqwā wa-yanbut rīshuh fa-yaʿūd ilayh abawāh fa-yarzuqānih] When the chicks come out of the egg, they (the parents) drive them away, because they come out exceedingly ugly to look at. For they have a small body, a large head and beak, a bare appearance, and the limbs of the body disjointed and badly knit together. So the parents, seeing the chick in such a state, desert it. But God most high gives it flies and gnats for food; this food is in the nest until (the chick) gains strength and its feathers grow, and the parents return to it and it is fed by them. To confirm this, another Arab, named Chalpholachmar, describes the foulness of the raven's chicks thus: رايت فرخ الغراب فلم ار صورة اقبح منه ولا اسمج الا اقذر ولا اشر رايت راسا كبيرا ومنقارا طويلا وذلك مع صغر البدن وصغر الجناح وهو امرط نتن الريح [raʾaytu farkh al-ghurāb fa-lam ara ṣūra aqbaḥ minhu wa-lā asmaj al-ā aqdhar wa-lā asharr raʾaytu raʾsan kabīran wa-minqāran ṭawīlan wa-dhālika maʿa ṣighar al-badan wa-ṣighar al-janāḥ wa-huwa amraṭ natin al-rīḥ] I saw a raven's chick, and I have never beheld anything fouler, more misshapen, more unclean or more vile. I saw a large head and a long beak, with a small body and small wings. It was also bare and of fetid breath, etc. There is no time to copy out more from the writings of the Arabs, and these suffice abundantly. So I shall add only this: among the ancient doctors of the church too there were some who embellished this fable in much the same way. Chrysostom, in the Sermon On Elias: Κεχηνότες εἰς ἀέρα τῶν κοράκων οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καὶ παρὰ τῶν γονέων μὴ τρεφόμενοι, ἔχουσιν αὐτοὶ ζῶα μικρά τινα τὴν θείαν ἐπιπέμπουσαν πρόνοιαν διακονούμενα· καὶ οὕτως ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐκεῖνα δεχόμενοι πρὸς αὔξησιν τρέφονται· [Kechēnotes eis aera tōn korakōn hoi neossoi, kai para tōn goneōn mē trephomenoi, echousin autoi zōa mikra tina tēn theian epipempousan pronoian diakonoumena; kai houtōs ek tou aeros ekeina dechomenoi pros auxēsin trephontai] The ravens' chicks, gaping into the air, since they are not fed by their parents, have certain tiny creatures which serve the providence of God, by whom they are sent; and receiving these from the air, they are nourished until they grow up. Olympiodorus on Job: Λέγεται ὁ κόραξ μὴ ἐκτρέφειν τὰ ἔκγονα ὑπὸ λαιμαργίας, ἀλλ᾽ ἀτημελήτους ἐᾶν τοὺς νεοσσούς· τοὺς δὲ, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνδείας πιεζομένους, φυσικῇ τινι κεχρῆσθαι πρὸς Θεὸν τῇ βοῇ, καὶ ὑπὸ μικρῶν τινων ζωϋφίων, γινομένων ἐν ταῖς νεοσσιαῖς, ἐκτρέφεσθαι. [Legetai ho korax mē ektrephein ta ekgona hypo laimargias, all᾽ atēmelētous ean tous neossous; tous de, hypo tēs endeias piezomenous, physikē tini kechrēsthai pros Theon tē boē, kai hypo mikrōn tinōn zōyphiōn, ginomenōn en tais neossiais, ektrephesthai] The raven is said, out of gluttony, not to rear its offspring, but to abandon its chicks uncared for; and they, pressed by hunger, use a kind of natural cry to God, and are nourished by certain small creatures which are born in the nests. Gregory on Job, book 30: When its chicks are hatched (the raven), as is reported, neglects to provide them food before they turn black by growing feathers, and lets them suffer hunger [II, 798] until its own likeness is seen in them through the blackness of their feathers. They wander here and there in the nest and seek the help of food with open mouth. But when they have begun to turn black, it seeks the food to be given them all the more eagerly, the longer it has put off feeding them. Isidore, Etymologies book 12, ch. 7: This bird is said [col. 207] not to give its hatched chicks full food until it recognizes in them the blackness of the feathers, the likeness of its own colour. But after it has seen them foul (I would prefer black) with feathers, having recognized them wholly, it feeds them more abundantly. Cassiodorus on the Psalms, and the author who circulates under the name of Jerome, say that the chicks, thus neglected, are fed by heavenly dew, which is the food of cicadas, not of ravens. But who would believe that flies and gnats are born in a raven's nest in such abundance as to suffice to feed several chicks, and very greedy ones at that? And that the gnats, as soon as they are born, of their own accord thrust themselves into the chicks' mouths to be devoured? Or that the parents hate their chicks because they are born partly featherless, when the very same thing happens to other birds? Or that, having once deserted them, they return to them as soon as they are clothed with feathers, or when these are blacker, as if someone had told them that their chicks are now in better shape and there is no longer reason to shrink from them? In a word, this is certain and already a common saying: to no bird is its own nest foul; and there is no animal that is not pleased by the form of its like. Hence Epicharmus in Laertius, in the Life of Plato:
— — — Καὶ γὰρ ὁ κύων κυνὶ Κάλλιστον εἶναι φαίνεται, καὶ βοῦς βοΐ, ῎Ονος δ᾽ ὄνῳ κάλλιστον, ὗς δ᾽ ὑΐ· [Kai gar ho kyōn kyni kalliston einai phainetai, kai bous boi, onos d᾽ onō kalliston, hys d᾽ hyi]

For to a dog a dog seems the most beautiful thing, and an ox to an ox, an ass to an ass, a pig to a pig. And Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods book 1: Do you think there is any beast on land or sea that does not take the greatest delight in a beast of its own kind? If it were not so, why would a bull not long to touch a mare, or a stallion a cow? Or do you suppose that an eagle, or a lion, or a dolphin prefers any shape to its own? So the Hebrews and the Arabs talk nonsense when they keep saying that the raven shrinks from its newly hatched chicks because they are wonderfully ugly. For if τὰ κορακίδια [ta korakidia] look vile to us, it does not follow that they look vile also to their parents, who view them with other eyes. And indeed, although these fables were invented solely to explain Scripture, they in no way agree with the words of Scripture. For Job does not say that the chicks of the ravens cry to God in the nest, but when they wander and stray about for lack of food. The subject, therefore, is chicks that have already left the nest. For that chicks should wander here and there within the nest itself, as Gregory says, cannot be conceived; the narrowness of a nest does not allow such wandering of the chicks. Nor in fact does the raven neglect its young while they are in the nest; rather, once they are fully reared and able to fly, it drives them from the nest, so that thereafter they may provide for themselves. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 31: Οἱ δὲ κόρακες τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεοττοὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσιν ἤδη πέτεσθαι, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκβάλλουσιν, [II, 799] ὕστερον δὲ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τόπου ἐκδιώκουσι· [Hoi de korakes tous heautōn neottous, hotan hoioi t᾽ ōsin ēdē petesthai, to men prōton ekballousin, hysteron de kai ek tou topou ekdiōkousi] But ravens, when their chicks are now able to fly, first cast them out of the nest, then drive them out of the whole district. Pliny, book 10, ch. 12, on the crow: This bird alone even feeds its chicks for some time after they can fly. All the others of the same kind drive their chicks from the nests and force them to fly, as do the ravens too, which drive each of their young, once strong, farther away. Aelian, On Animals book 2, ch. 49: Τούς γε μὴν νεοττοὺς τοὺς ἐκτραφέντας διώκουσι, καὶ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιᾶς φυγάδας ἀποφαίνουσιν ὑπὲρ ὅτου τροφὰς μαστεύουσι. [Tous ge mēn neottous tous ektraphentas diōkousi, kai tēs heautōn hekastos kalias phygadas apophainousin hyper hotou trophas masteuousi.] Their chicks, indeed, once reared, they chase away; and each drives them from its nest, for which reason the chicks thereafter seek their own food. It is only when the chicks have been cast out in this way, then, that there happens [col. 208] what the sacred writer relates: that, wandering for lack of food, they as it were cry to God. For since they are not yet at full strength, nor in the perfect vigour of their age, and have not yet grown used to procuring food for themselves by their own effort and industry, they are utterly at a loss, croak loudly, and fill the air with plaintive cries, as though complaining to God of their parents' ἀστοργία [astorgia]. And in these straits God comes to their aid, not by miraculously producing flies and gnats that thrust themselves of their own accord into their mouths, but by suggesting to them what must be done and how to provide against pressing hunger, so that they do not perish of starvation. Thus the same thing happens here to the chicks of ravens as to the whelps of lions, which, deserted by their mother, lack and suffer hunger, Psal. XXXIV, 11, and roar after their prey, as though seeking their food from God, Psal. CIV, 21. And God satisfies them, Iob. XXXIX, 1 (var. XXXVIII, 39). Yet one need not trouble much over why this is attributed to the chicks of ravens rather than to the ravens themselves, since Christ said it of ravens too, Luc. XII, 24: Consider the ravens, which neither sow etc. and yet God feeds them. Nor was there any reason for the Arabic translator to render ravens as فراخا الغربان [firākhā al-ghirbān] chicks of ravens. For a translator may not change anything in the words of the sacred text unless necessity compels him, and here no such necessity appears, since Christ says nothing of ravens that does not suit the whole species. Consider, he says, the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. This is as true of the parents as of the chicks: neither sows or reaps; neither has storerooms or barns. Finally, God provides for both alike. Indeed, Christ applies these same words to all birds, Matth. VI, 26: Consider, he says, the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap etc. But what he asserts there of birds in general he narrows, Matth. X, 29, to sparrows, which, though very cheap and sold two for a farthing, God nevertheless does not judge unworthy of his care. And in Luc. XII, 24 he extends the same to ravens too, which, ugly birds though they are, harsh of voice and of ill omen, he nevertheless does not disdain to feed. So nothing peculiar is attributed here to ravens or to the chicks of ravens. Rather, they, like the sparrows, are expressly mentioned among the other birds, to make clear that God's providence not only cares for birds in general, but extends even to the cheapest and most despised of them, [II, 800] so that men, and faithful men above all, may conclude the more surely that they are in God's care: what he so kindly grants to little creatures of the lowest order, he will not deny to those by whom he is worshipped and invoked. Having explained these things thus, I will not conceal that in Servius, in his Notes on book 1 of the Georgics, one reads this: Pliny in his Natural History says that ravens are forgetful and for the most part do not return to their nests at all; but by a certain provision of nature they gather at their nests things that can produce worms, by which their abandoned chicks are sometimes fed. Hence it may seem that the fable we have refuted can be confirmed by the authority of Pliny. But there is no reason for this to trouble anyone. For Servius either deceives or is deceived, since nothing of the kind is read either in Pliny or in any of the philosophers who preceded the age of Servius. So this is a mere dream from the ivory gate, of the sort that learned men have already observed slipped from him in large numbers.
